title: Open a Hole, Spend the Gradient

scenes.tts: How can a cell answer a signal in about a millisecond? Most receptors hand their message to a G protein or a kinase. An ion channel skips that chain: the signal opens a hole, ions rush through, and voltage shifts at once.
scenes.caption: How can a cell answer a signal in about a millisecond? Most receptors hand their message to a G protein or a kinase. An ion channel skips that chain: the signal opens a hole, ions rush through, and voltage shifts at once.
scenes.visual: Deep slate background (#0F172A). Full-width horizontal lipid bilayer across the middle (Outside above, Inside below), filling 60% of frame height. Ambient drifting ions: warm amber Na+ crowded outside, bright teal K+ crowded inside. A silver-blue channel sits closed in the membrane beside a tall vertical voltage gauge on the right (marked schematic, resting white needle at −70 mV). As narration ends, a brief flash opens the gate and amber ions stream down while the white needle jumps upward.
scenes.narration: How can a cell answer a signal in about a millisecond? Most receptors hand their message to a G protein or a kinase. An ion channel skips that chain: the signal opens a hole, ions rush through, and voltage shifts at once.

scenes.visual: Hold the drifting membrane world softly dimmed behind clean high-contrast title text (size 48, white): 'Open a Hole, Spend the Gradient'. Ions keep drifting gently so the frame stays alive.

scenes.tts: Two kinds of protein move ions across a membrane. A pump binds ions, uses A T P, and pushes them uphill, only a few hundred each second. A channel is a gated pore. Open it, and millions pour downhill every second. Pumps build gradients slowly; channels spend them fast.
scenes.caption: Two kinds of protein move ions across a membrane. A pump binds ions, uses ATP, and pushes them uphill, only a few hundred each second. A channel is a gated pore. Open it, and millions pour downhill every second. Pumps build gradients slowly; channels spend them fast.
scenes.visual: Same bilayer world, now showing two proteins side by side. Left: a pump labelled 'Pump (ATP)' slowly cycling shape to push amber Na+ up and teal K+ down, with a live counter ticking '~10² ions/s'. Right: a gated channel labelled 'Open channel' letting a dense stream of ions rush straight through, counter spinning '~10⁷ ions/s'. Both counters and ion streams animate continuously while the narrator speaks.
scenes.narration: Two kinds of protein move ions across a membrane. A pump binds ions, uses ATP, and pushes them uphill, only a few hundred each second. A channel is a gated pore. Open it, and millions pour downhill every second. Pumps build gradients slowly; channels spend them fast.

scenes.tts: What makes an ion run downhill through an open pore? Two forces. Crowded ions spread from high concentration toward low. Membrane voltage pulls on their charge; a resting neuron sits about minus seventy millivolts inside. Together, they form the electrochemical gradient.
scenes.caption: What makes an ion run downhill through an open pore? Two forces. Crowded ions spread from high concentration toward low. Membrane voltage pulls on their charge; a resting neuron sits about −70 mV inside. Together, they form the electrochemical gradient.
scenes.visual: The pump fades away; the carried membrane and right-hand voltage gauge stay in place (needle steady at '−70 mV (rest)', minus signs glowing gently along the inner bilayer face). On the left, a thick arrow labelled 'Concentration push' points from crowded outside ions downward. Beside it, an electric-field arrow labelled 'Voltage pull' points toward the negative interior. Both arrows merge into one highlighted bracket labelled 'Electrochemical gradient'.
scenes.narration: What makes an ion run downhill through an open pore? Two forces. Crowded ions spread from high concentration toward low. Membrane voltage pulls on their charge; a resting neuron sits about −70 mV inside. Together, they form the electrochemical gradient.

scenes.tts: For each ion, one membrane voltage balances those two forces exactly. That balance point is its equilibrium potential. Sodium is crowded outside, so only a strongly positive inside, about plus sixty millivolts, holds it back. Potassium is crowded inside, so its balance point, about minus ninety, sits below rest.
scenes.caption: For each ion, one membrane voltage balances those two forces exactly. That balance point is its equilibrium potential. Na+ is crowded outside, so only a strongly positive inside, about +60 mV, holds it back. K+ is crowded inside, so its balance point, about −90 mV, sits below rest.
scenes.visual: Focus stays on the membrane and the vertical voltage gauge (schematic scale from −100 mV to +80 mV). First, amber Na+ crowds above the pore while the gauge highlights an amber tick at 'E_Na ≈ +60 mV'; opposing inward concentration and outward electrical arrows shrink to equal length (net flow zero). Next, teal K+ crowds below the pore while the gauge highlights a teal tick at 'E_K ≈ −90 mV', again showing equal opposing arrows.
scenes.narration: For each ion, one membrane voltage balances those two forces exactly. That balance point is its equilibrium potential. Na+ is crowded outside, so only a strongly positive inside, about +60 mV, holds it back. K+ is crowded inside, so its balance point, about −90 mV, sits below rest.

scenes.tts: Here is the core rule. An open channel pulls membrane voltage toward its ion’s equilibrium potential. The pull is the driving force: membrane voltage minus equilibrium potential. For sodium, minus seventy minus sixty is minus one hundred thirty millivolts, a huge gap. For potassium, minus seventy minus minus ninety is just twenty.
scenes.caption: Here is the core rule. An open channel pulls membrane voltage toward its ion’s equilibrium potential. The pull is the driving force: membrane voltage minus equilibrium potential. For Na+, −70 − (+60) = −130 mV, a huge gap. For K+, −70 − (−90) = just +20 mV.
scenes.visual: Same membrane and voltage gauge, needle resting at 'Vm = −70 mV'. A formula card appears top left as the narrator says it: 'Driving force = Vm − E'. Two vertical driving-force brackets then grow along the gauge as each number is spoken: a long amber bracket from −70 mV up to E_Na (+60 mV), labelled 'Na+: −70 − (+60) = −130 mV'; and a short teal bracket from −70 mV down to E_K (−90 mV), labelled 'K+: −70 − (−90) = +20 mV'. Both brackets pulse gently in proportion to their length.

scenes.tts: Picture a resting neuron with two closed channels: one for sodium, one for potassium. Pause and predict. If we open each in turn, which ion rushes harder? And which way does voltage move each time?
scenes.caption: Picture a resting neuron with two closed channels: one for Na+, one for K+. Pause and predict. If we open each in turn, which ion rushes harder? And which way does voltage move each time?
scenes.visual: In the same bilayer, an amber-trimmed Na+ channel and a teal-trimmed K+ channel sit side by side, both closed. The right-hand gauge needle sits steady at −70 mV with E_Na (+60 mV) and E_K (−90 mV) ticks visible. A clean top prompt card fades in: 'Predict: Which ion rushes harder, and which way does Vm move?'
scenes.narration: Picture a resting neuron with two closed channels: one for Na+, one for K+. Pause and predict. If we open each in turn, which ion rushes harder? And which way does voltage move each time?

scenes.visual: Keep the prompt card, both closed channels, and the voltage gauge on screen for thinking time. Amber Na+ outside and teal K+ inside drift slowly in ambient motion; a thin subtle progress bar glides across the bottom of the prompt card.

scenes.tts: Sodium’s gap is huge, so it pours inward and voltage shoots upward. Each ion carries positive charge in, making the inside less negative; that is depolarisation. Now shut sodium and open potassium. Its gap is small, so potassium leaks out gently. Losing positive charge nudges the voltage slightly downward.
scenes.caption: Na+’s gap is huge, so it pours inward and voltage shoots upward. Each ion carries positive charge in, making the inside less negative; that is depolarisation. Now shut Na+ and open K+. Its gap is small, so K+ leaks out gently. Losing positive charge nudges the voltage slightly downward.
scenes.visual: Prompt card clears. First, the amber Na+ channel swings open: a rapid dense torrent of amber ions enters the cell while the white gauge needle shoots upward toward +60 mV (label 'Depolarisation'). Then the Na+ channel shuts and Vm returns to −70 mV. Next, the teal K+ channel opens: a gentle sparse stream of teal ions exits upward while the white needle nudges slightly downward toward −90 mV.
scenes.narration: Na+’s gap is huge, so it pours inward and voltage shoots upward. Each ion carries positive charge in, making the inside less negative; that is depolarisation. Now shut Na+ and open K+. Its gap is small, so K+ leaks out gently. Losing positive charge nudges the voltage slightly downward.

scenes.tts: A glass pipette sealed onto a membrane patch, the patch clamp, records one channel at a time. The current jumps between shut and open at a fixed height. A stronger signal does not widen the pore. Instead, it raises the share of time the channel spends open.

scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly on one channel in the same bilayer while a schematic single-channel current trace scrolls live beneath it (labelled 'Single-channel current (schematic)', levels 'Closed' and 'Open'). Every time the gate snaps open, a burst of ions crosses and the trace jumps cleanly to the same square plateau. A small signal slider rises from 'Weak' to 'Strong': the step height stays identical while open bursts grow more frequent.

scenes.tts: Few ions need to cross, because a thin membrane turns a tiny charge imbalance into a large voltage. Bulk concentrations barely shift, and nothing new is made. A channel passing several ions pulls voltage between their equilibrium potentials. Spend the stored gradient, and voltage becomes a fast signal.

scenes.visual: Pull back to the full bilayer world. A single channel flickers open: the white Vm needle makes a bold upward swing while two small concentration meters ('Bulk Na+ out', 'Bulk K+ in') stay virtually flat. Briefly show a neutral multi-ion channel passing both amber and teal ions with the target marker sitting between E_K and E_Na, then fade smoothly toward the end card.
